title: Nucleolar Compartments Visualized by Atomic Force Microscopy
content: The nucleolus is a plurifunctional intranuclear membrane-less organelle where synthesis and processing of pre-rRNA as well as ribosome assembly take place [1] and is considered also as a nuclear condensate [2]. It is composed of three different ultrastructural elements known as fibrillar centers, dense fibrillar and granular components. In addition, the nucleolus contains more than 700 proteins, pre-rRNA, rRNA, rDNA and several UsnoRNAs. The nucleolus has been observed in all eukaryote cells including plants, animals, fungi and protists as the unicellular parasite Giardia lamblia [3] and even recently, a structure similar to this organelle was described in a member of the group archaea [4]. To characterize nucleolar components at nanoscale, we use animal and plant cells processed as for transmission electron microscopy. Briefly, samples of Gingko biloba leaves and Hep2 cells were fixed with 6% glutaraldehyde and 4% paraformaldehyde and postfixed with 1% osmium tetroxide. Dehydration was conducted with a graded series of ethanol and propylene oxide. Embedding was carried out in epoxy resin polymerized at 60oC. Semithin sections were mounted in glass slides and scanned with an atomic force microscope operating in contact mode, as previously described [5]. Thin sections were also obtained and mounted in formvar-coated cupper grids, the stained with uranyl acetate and lead citrate, and observed in a transmission electron microscope operating at 80 kV. Atomic force results indicate that dense fibrillar and granular components display different nanometric surface profiles (Fig. 1), different from those of the cytoplasm and other regions within the cell nucleus. We propose that nucleolar profiles obtained by atomic force microscopy on semithin sections of resin embedded samples mounted on glass slides may be used to analyze nucleolar structure under different physiological conditions.
